The Unreasonable Effectiveness of HTML for AI Agents
item.description:
Thariq Shihipar, the engineering lead for Claude Code at Anthropic, published a blog post that hit 4.4 million views in 16 hours arguing that HTML outperforms Markdown for AI agent outputs. The argument is practical: as agents handle larger tasks, Markdown walls of text become impossible to review. HTML gives agents tables, SVG diagrams, interactive navigation, and copy buttons that make output reviewable and actionable. Twenty working examples back the claim. Combined with dynamic workflows — the Opus 4.8 feature that orchestrates up to 1,000 subagents in a single JavaScript script — HTML artifacts become durable project context rather than disposable chat output. The bottleneck is no longer code generation speed but the interface through which humans stay cognitively connected to what agents produce.
Links: https://claude.com/blog/using-claude-code-the-unreasonable-effectiveness-of-html https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows https://thariqs.github.io/html-effectiveness/

item.title: Uganda Real Estate Investment for Foreigners
item.description:
Uganda offers 7 to 9 percent gross rental yields in Kampala's mid-market suburbs with entry prices around 70 to 95 thousand US dollars — but foreigners cannot own freehold land, only leasehold up to 99 years. Title fraud is endemic, the market is illiquid, and President Museveni has been in power since 1986 with no succession plan. After rental income tax at 12 percent of gross with no expense deductions, property management, maintenance, and vacancy, your net yield drops to 4 to 6 percent in shillings. Subtract currency drift and you land at 5 to 9 percent net in dollars on a good day — roughly what Ugandan treasury bonds pay without any of the headaches. The play is condominium units with clean registered titles, all-cash, sized small, with the exit planned at entry. The demographics are undeniable. The government's hand is heavy.
Links: https://juruga.org/constitution/article/237/land-ownership https://ulii.org/akn/ug/act/2001/4/eng@2001-02-23/source https://www.ugandainvest.go.ug/

item.title: Robinhood Is Now Open to Agents
item.description:
Robinhood just opened its platform to AI agents through a new MCP server that lets autonomous software trade stocks, manage portfolios, and move money without a single button click. The architecture uses the Model Context Protocol — an open standard for connecting AI models to external tools — meaning any compatible agent can connect to your brokerage account. The upside is real: automation previously reserved for quant funds is now available to retail investors. The danger is equally real: every API is a potential vulnerability, and when an AI agent has discretion over your portfolio, prompt injection becomes a financial weapon. The SEC is circling algorithmic trading with new scrutiny on algorithmic collusion and explainability requirements, but nobody has answered the fundamental question — when an AI agent makes a bad trade, who is liable? Robinhood frames this as democratizing finance. A more honest reading is that agents don't get cold feet, don't panic sell, and generate trading volume that feeds Robinhood's revenue model. This is the inevitable future of autonomous finance. The infrastructure choices made now will shape how it works for decades.
Links: https://robinhood.com/us/en/newsroom/robinhood-is-now-open-to-agents/ https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/daly-020326-artificial-intelligence-future-investment-management https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18

item.title: The History of Taxation: From Ancient Tribute to Modern Certainty
item.description:
Taxation may be the second-oldest profession — and it has always worked the same way. From Egyptian grain tributes assessed by the scribe of the treasury around 3000 BCE, through Roman tax farmers called publicani who bid at auction for the right to extract whatever they could from provincials, to Magna Carta Clause 12 in 1215 which established no tax without common counsel — extracted at sword-point from King John, not granted by legal philosophy. William Pitt the Younger introduced British income tax in 1799 at 10 percent on incomes above 200 pounds, promised it was temporary, and it was repealed after Waterloo. Robert Peel brought it back in 1842 and it has never left. The US 16th Amendment in 1913 started at 1 percent on incomes above $3,000 with a top rate of 7 percent. By 1918 the top rate hit 77 percent. The Spanish-American War telephone tax of 1898 lasted 108 years. The window tax of 1696 made people brick up their windows for 150 years. Every major tax was sold as temporary. Every one became permanent. The pattern: crisis creates urgency, the tax is introduced with sunset promises, the crisis passes, the revenue proves too convenient, and the sunset clause quietly fails. Legality and legitimacy are not the same thing. The history of taxation is not a history of consent — it is a history of expedience becoming permanent.

item.title: Karpathy's LLM Wiki: Build Your Own Knowledge Base
item.description:
Andrej Karpathy published a single GitHub Gist called llm-wiki.md that reframes personal knowledge management using the oldest trick in software engineering: compilation. Your raw sources are source code, the wiki is the compiled binary, and the AI is the compiler. The three-layer architecture keeps raw sources immutable at the bottom, an AI-owned wiki of entity pages, concept pages, and cross-links in the middle, and a schema file like CLAUDE.md at the top that turns a generic agent into a disciplined wiki maintainer. Three operations power the whole thing: ingest drops a source and the AI updates 10 to 15 pages at once, query reads the pre-synthesised wiki instead of raw documents, and lint audits for contradictions, orphans, and stale data. Knowledge compounds over time rather than starting from scratch on every query. The pattern echoes Garry Tan's GBrain system indexing 146,000 pages and the Hermes agent's own llm-wiki skill with Obsidian. The deeper lineage goes back to Vannevar Bush's 1945 Memex vision — a personal knowledge store where connections between documents matter as much as the documents themselves. The bookkeeping that killed every previous wiki is exactly what AI automates. Your knowledge stays on your machine, in markdown, with no cloud dependency and no vendor lock-in.

item.title: GBrain: Garry Tan's AI Knowledge System That Makes You Wake Up Smarter
item.description: Garry Tan, President of Y Combinator, personally built GBrain — an open-source AI knowledge system with 147,000 indexed pages, 25,000 tracked people, and 5,000 companies. Unlike traditional knowledge tools that return lists of pages, GBrain synthesizes actual answers with gap analysis telling you what it doesn't know yet. Three pillars make it work: hybrid search with a synthesis layer, a self-wiring knowledge graph that creates typed edges with zero LLM calls, and a dream cycle that enriches your brain while you sleep. Nearly 20,000 GitHub stars. The deeper question: does a 25-year-old with GBrain running for two years have better institutional memory than a 50-year-old executive relying on recall?

item.description: Vit Jedlicka warns that global government is the most dangerous concept humanity is playing with — borders are not just arbitrary lines but limits on power. Liberland funds itself through voluntary merit purchases instead of taxes, runs elections every three months on blockchain, and plans to let AI agents hold governance shares. Eight hundred thousand citizenship applications, Justin Sun as a citizen, and a diaspora network spanning every continent. The question is not whether Liberland succeeds but whether the idea spreads fast enough before the global bureaucrats finish building their cage.

item.title: Can One Ancient Hum Really Awaken the Pineal Gland?
item.description: By age forty, there's a seventy percent chance your pineal gland has started calcifying. By fifty-five, it's over eighty percent. Yet an ancient yogic technique called Brahmari — just three minutes of daily humming — may reverse this. Researchers at the Karinolinska Institute found that humming increases nitric oxide production fifteen-fold, and that molecule can reach the pineal gland through the cribriform plate to dissolve calcified deposits. The same mechanism cardiologists have used for decades to clear arterial plaque, applied to the most enigmatic gland in the human brain.

item.title: The Anarchist Who Tried to Destroy Marx's Movement
item.description: Mikhail Bakunin was born into Russian nobility and discarded every privilege for revolutionary activism. Karl Marx believed the working class should seize the state; Bakunin believed the state itself was the trap. The International collapsed within four years. A century later, Bakunin's warning — that revolutionaries who inherit state machinery become the new tyrants — was borne out across every Marxist revolution of the twentieth century.

item.title: Subqueue Claims 52x Faster Long-Context AI With Sub-Quadratic Attention
item.description: A Miami-based startup called Subqueue claims to have built a model with a 12 million token context window using Sub-Quadratic Sparse Attention, or SSA. Rather than attending to every token, the model skims the query, decides which tokens matter, and only attends to those, turning a quadratic cost problem into a linear one. The company says it runs 52 times faster than Flash Attention at one-fifth the cost. But there are no published technical reports, no independent verification, and no benchmarks for the headline 12 million token claim. With former Meta and Google engineers on the team, the pedigree is there but the evidence is not — yet.

item.title: This Home Costs $300 to Build and $0 to Heat FOREVER. Why Is It Banned?

Each brick costs three cents, walls maintain stable temperatures without any mechanical system, and a University of Arizona study showed adobe homes needed zero cooling while wood-frame homes ran air conditioning ten months a year. The codes were written by the Portland Cement Association, an $18 billion industry protecting its market. But legal loopholes exist, and Simone Swan used them to build 600 adobe homes for families earning under $12,000 a year — with zero energy bills and no mortgage.

item.title: What the Founding Fathers of Israel Actually Said Behind Closed Doors
item.description: Historical documents and statements from Israel's own founding figures paint a more complicated picture than the standard narrative suggests. Ben-Gurion called partition a temporary strategy. Weizmann said it would only last 25 to 30 years. Accounts of the 1948 conflict include allegations of deliberate provocation, systematic brutality, and whisper propaganda designed to spread fear. The same patterns of contested narratives and resistance to scrutiny echo into the present, shaping how we see the conflict today.
